title: Attributes the compiler and CLR actually honor
hook: Attributes attach metadata to assemblies, types, and members. Some are pure documentation; others change compiler behavior, serialization, validation, or run-time code paths — like [Required], [JsonPropertyName], or [Obsolete].

blocks.text: An attribute is a class deriving from System.Attribute applied in square brackets. The compiler stores attribute instances in metadata. Frameworks read them via reflection or source generators: ASP.NET Core reads [HttpGet], System.Text.Json reads [JsonIgnore], nullable reference types use [NotNullWhen]. Custom attributes can drive your own tooling if you read them at compile time or run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Metadata annotation on code elements, stored in assembly metadata.
Declares which targets a custom attribute can apply to.
Marks a member as deprecated; compiler can warn or error.

blocks.text: Auth tokens and API contracts often use attributes for validation ([Authorize], [Required], [MaxLength]). Serialization shape is attribute-driven in many stacks. Interviewers ask which attributes are compile-time versus run-time — [Conditional] is compile-time; [Serializable] is mostly legacy.

blocks.title: Compiler vs framework
blocks.body: The C# compiler understands a small set (Obsolete, Conditional, Nullable attributes). Most framework attributes are read by libraries at run time or by source generators at compile time.

snippet.label: Custom attribute definition
snippet.explanation: Define reusable metadata. Your feature system reads it via reflection or a generator.

snippet.label: Obsolete with compile-time enforcement
snippet.explanation: Compiler honors Obsolete directly — error:true blocks call sites without any runtime check.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Attributes on properties that nothing reads — dead metadata. Wrong AttributeTargets so attribute does not compile on method. Assuming [Serializable] replaces proper DTO design in modern APIs.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: attributes compile into metadata tables — ildasm or dotPeek shows them on types and members. The C# compiler directly honors Obsolete, Conditional, and nullable flow attributes; ASP.NET and System.Text.Json read their attributes at startup via reflection or source generators. Dead attributes bloat metadata and confuse readers — grep for GetCustomAttribute consumers before adding new ones. Nullable and DynamicallyAccessedMembers attributes feed trim and analyzer pipelines in CI.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming all attributes are compiler magic — most are passive metadata until a framework reads them. Putting validation attributes on fields when the validator only inspects properties. Mixing Newtonsoft and System.Text.Json attribute sets on the same DTO. Custom attributes with no consumer — dead weight in every assembly.

interviewTakeaways: Attributes are IL metadata; the compiler honors Obsolete, Conditional, and nullable attributes — frameworks read the rest via reflection or generators.
Validation and JSON attributes on DTOs must match what the framework actually inspects — property vs field targets matter.
In production, audit custom attributes — if nothing reads them at startup or compile time, remove them to shrink metadata.
60s: Attributes are metadata tables. Compiler: Obsolete, Conditional, nullable. Frameworks: validation, JSON, routing. Generators replace runtime attribute scanning on hot paths.
Follow-up: how do source generators read attributes without runtime reflection?
commonPitfalls: Saying the compiler enforces [Required] gets you rejected — ASP.NET/model binders read it at runtime.
Custom attributes never consumed by reflection or a generator.
Strong answer: 'Compiler attributes vs framework attributes. Generators for hot paths. Match attribute target to consumer. Obsolete error:true for hard breaks.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS decorators attach metadata similar to C# attributes but rely on emit helpers. C# stores attributes in CLR metadata tables.
JSDoc @deprecated is comment-only — no compile enforcement. C# [Obsolete(error:true)] is a hard compiler error.
